facts.text: Galla Placidia was forced by her brother Honorius into marriage with Constantius III, his magister militum.
Having been pardoned by Eudokia Makrembolitissa, the regent of the Byzantine Empire, for attempting to usurp the throne, Romanos IV Diogenes married her to become Byzantine emperor.
Bouvet Island in the South Atlantic Ocean, the most remote island in the world, was discovered by French explorer Jean-Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier.
The hymn " Amazing Grace " was probably first used in a prayer meeting in Olney, England, without the music familiar to modern listeners.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of his chorale cantata Jesu, nun sei gepreiset, which features trumpet fanfares at the start and end.
Quasi-War: An American convoy of four merchant vessels escorted by a schooner was attacked by a squadron of armed barges manned by Haitians.
Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered the dwarf planet Ceres, naming it after the Roman goddess of agriculture and of motherly love.
As a result of the lobbying efforts by the abolitionist movement, the importation of slaves into the United States was officially banned, although slavery itself remained permitted.

image.caption: Long title An Act to prohibit the importation of slaves, into any port or place within the jurisdiction of the United States, from and after the first day of January, in the year of our Lord, One Thousand Eight Hundred and Eight.

facts.text: Lachlan Macquarie became Governor of New South Wales, eventually playing a major role in the social, economic and architectural development of the colony in Australia.
The immigration station on Ellis Island in New York Harbor opened, and would process almost 12 million immigrants to the United States over the course of its existence.

image.caption: Location Upper New York Bay Jersey City, New Jersey , and New York City , New York United States

facts.text: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line in the U.S. state of Florida became the first scheduled airline using a winged aircraft.
Russia withdraws from its occupation of northwestern Iran, enabling a subsequent Ottoman invasion and massacres of Assyrians and Armenians.
Joseph Stalin 's personal secretary, Boris Bazhanov, crossed the Iranian border and defected from the Soviet Union.
World War II: In retaliation for the massacre of captured Americans by Waffen SS soldiers, U.S. Army personnel killed an estimated 80 Wehrmacht prisoners near Chenogne, Belgium.
Second World War: The Luftwaffe launched Operation Bodenplatte in an attempt to cripple Allied air forces in the Low Countries.
British Railways came into existence when the " Big Four " railway companies were nationalised.
The revised Thai criminal code came into force, strengthening the law on lèse-majesté in Thailand to include insult and treating it as a crime against national security.
Three men were killed and two wounded in a mass shooting at a public house in Sheffield, England.
The People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan, which later helped the country become a republic, was founded.
Air India Flight 855 crashed into the Arabian Sea seconds after take-off, killing all 213 people.
The revolutionary leftist Zapatista Army of National Liberation initiated twelve days of armed conflict in the Mexican state of Chiapas.
The World Trade Organization, the international organization designed to supervise and liberalize international trade, came into being, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

links.title: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade

facts.text: Argentinian physicist Juan Maldacena published a landmark paper initiating the study of AdS/CFT correspondence, which links string theory and quantum gravity.
Adam Air Flight 574 crashed into the sea off Polewali, Indonesia, killing all 102 people on board, when the pilots inadvertently disconnected the autopilot.
A suicide bomber killed 105 spectators at a volleyball game in the Lakki Marwat District of Pakistan.
The NASA space probe New Horizons flew by the trans-Neptunian object Arrokoth, making it the farthest object visited by a spacecraft.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of Herr Gott, dich loben wir, BWV 16, his church cantata for New Year's Day to a libretto by Georg Christian Lehms.

links.title: Herr Gott, dich loben wir, BWV 16

facts.text: American Revolutionary War: The town of Norfolk, Virginia, was burned and destroyed by the combined actions of British and Whig forces.
The Times began publication in London as The Daily Universal Register.
Ireland's first broadcaster, 2RN, began broadcasting.
A suicide bombing took place outside a Coptic Orthodox Church in Alexandria, Egypt, following a New Year service, killing 23 people.
American Revolutionary War: American forces under the command of George Washington repulsed a British attack at the Battle of the Assunpink Creek near Trenton, New Jersey.
French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier announced the putative discovery of the planet Vulcan at a meeting at the French Academy of Sciences in Paris.
Uruguayan War: Brazilian and Colorado Party forces captured the city of Paysandú from its Uruguayan defenders.

Under the leadership of Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, U.S. Department of Justice agents launched a series of raids against radical leftists and anarchists in more than 30 cities and towns across 23 states.
World War II: United States and Australian forces successfully landed in Papua New Guinea in an attempt to cut off a Japanese retreat.
The Soviet Luna 1, the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of the Moon, was launched by a Vostok rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome.
Vietnam War: The Viet Cong won its first major victory at the Battle of Ap Bac.
Ronald Reagan began his career in government when he was sworn in as the 33rd governor of California.
Sharon Pratt Dixon was sworn in as the mayor of Washington, D.C., becoming the first African-American woman to hold the position.

links.title: Mayor of the District of Columbia

facts.text: The Stardust space probe flew by the comet Wild 2 and collected particle samples from its coma, which were later returned to Earth.
Sri Lankan civil war: The Sri Lankan army captured the town of Kilinochchi from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, concluding the Battle of Kilinochchi.
Nimr al-Nimr, a prominent Shia cleric in Saudi Arabia, was executed by the Saudi government along with 46 other people.
Mercurius, a Roman priest, was elected Pope John II; he was likely the first pope to adopt a new name upon elevation to the papacy.
Trunajaya rebellion: Amangkurat II of Mataram of Java and his courtiers stabbed Trunajaya to death a week after the rebel leader surrendered to VOC forces.
Second World War: Llandaff Cathedral in Cardiff, Wales, was severely damaged by German bombing during the Cardiff Blitz.
An extratropical cyclone began affecting parts of western Europe, resulting in coastal flooding around the southern portions of the North Sea and leading to at least 82 deaths.
While landing at Haneda Airport, Japan Airlines Flight 516 collided with a De Havilland Canada Dash 8 which killed five people in total.
Decius ordered all people in the Roman Empire (except Jews) to perform a sacrifice to the Roman gods, resulting in widespread persecution of Christians.
The first issue of Berlingske, Denmark's oldest continually operating newspaper, was published.
American Revolutionary War: American forces commanded by George Washington defeated British troops at the Battle of Princeton (depicted).
An earthquake registering 7.7 M w destroyed Almaty in Russian Turkestan.
The American health charity March of Dimes was founded as the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis to help raise money for polio research.
United States invasion of Panama: Manuel Noriega, the deposed strongman of Panama, surrendered to American forces outside the apostolic nunciature in Panama City.
Second Intifada: Israeli forces seized MV Karine A, which was carrying 50 tons of smuggled weapons on behalf of the Palestinian Authority.
Flash Airlines Flight 604 crashed shortly after departure from Sharm El Sheikh International Airport which killed all 148 occupants on board.
The cryptocurrency network of bitcoin was created when Satoshi Nakamoto mined the first block of the chain.
Pope Leo X issued the papal bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, excommunicating Martin Luther for refusing to retract 41 alleged errors found in his 95 Theses and other writings.
A gun battle in the East End of London left two dead and sparked a political row over the operational involvement of Winston Churchill, then Home Secretary.
Second World War: As part of Operation Compass, Australian and United Kingdom forces attacked Italian forces at the Battle of Bardia in Egypt.
All 25 people on board Aero Flight 311 died in Finland's worst civilian air accident when the aircraft crashed near Kvevlax.
CBS announced the sale of the New York Yankees professional baseball team to a group of investors headed by American businessman George Steinbrenner.
The United States launches a military operation in Venezuela, capturing president Nicolás Maduro and his wife.

image.caption: Location Northern Venezuela, including Greater Caracas

facts.text: Most of London's Palace of Whitehall, the main residence of English monarchs since 1530, was destroyed by fire.
Solomon Northup regained his freedom after having been sold into slavery in the American South; his memoir Twelve Years a Slave later became a bestseller.

image.caption: Born Solomon Northup [ a ] July 10, c. 1807–1808 Minerva, New York , U.S.

facts.text: Billboard published its first music hit parade.
A magnitude-7.1 earthquake occurred in Tonghai County, China, killing at least 15,000 people.
Last of the Summer Wine, the longest-running sitcom in the world, premiered as an episode of the BBC 's Comedy Playhouse.
The English punk-rock band Sex Pistols ' lewd and disruptive behaviour at Heathrow Airport prompted the record label EMI to end their contract.
Two American F-14 Tomcats shot down two Libyan MiG-23 Floggers that appeared to be attempting to engage them over the Gulf of Sidra.
Spirit (artist's impression depicted), the first of two rovers of NASA 's Mars Exploration Rover mission, successfully landed on Mars.
Nancy Pelosi became Speaker of the United States House of Representatives, becoming the highest-ranking woman in the history of the U.S. government.

links.title: Speaker of the United States House of Representatives
Federal government of the United States

facts.text: The Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest structure, officially opened in Dubai.
Sembawang Hot Spring Park in Singapore reopened after being redeveloped by the National Parks Board.
After his appointment as Prince of Wallachia, Constantine Hangerli arrived in Bucharest to assume the throne.
British explorer Aeneas Mackintosh, a member of the Nimrod Expedition, escaped death by fleeing across ice floes.
Korean War: Chinese and North Korean troops captured Seoul from United Nations forces.
Rose Heilbron became the first female judge to sit at the Central Criminal Court of England and Wales.
A fire in an escape room in Koszalin, Poland, killed five teenagers.
King Louis XV survived an assassination attempt by Robert-François Damiens, who later became the last person in France to be executed by drawing and quartering.
Te Kooti's War: After surviving a five-day siege in the pā at Ngātapa, Māori leader Te Kooti escaped from New Zealand's Armed Constabulary.
The German Workers' Party, the precursor of the Nazi Party, was founded by Anton Drexler.
Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton died of a heart attack during his final expedition.
Construction began on the Golden Gate Bridge across the Straits of the Golden Gate, the entrance to San Francisco Bay.
Second World War: Australian and British troops defeated Italian forces in Bardia, Libya, the first battle of the war in which an Australian Army formation took part.
In his State of the Union speech, U.S. president Harry S. Truman announced: "Every segment of our population, and every individual, has a right to expect from his government a fair deal."
A magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck Tonghai County in southern China, killing at least 10,000 people and eventually spurring the creation of the nation's largest earthquake monitoring system.
Georgian troops attacked Tskhinvali, the South Ossetian capital, beginning the First South Ossetia War.
Sri Lankan Tamil politician Kumar Ponnambalam was killed in an assassination suspected to have been sanctioned by President Chandrika Kumaratunga.
The Metropolitan Police arrested six people in conjunction with an alleged terrorist plot to release ricin on the London Underground, although no toxin was found.
The dwarf planet Eris was discovered by a team using images from the Samuel Oschin telescope at Palomar Observatory.
The Taiwan High Speed Rail opened, connecting Taipei and Kaohsiung.
Mikheil Saakashvili was decisively re-elected as President of Georgia in "the first genuinely competitive presidential election" in the history of the country.
In Eng Foong Ho v Attorney-General, the Court of Appeal of Singapore held that equality before the law was satisfied by a "reasonable nexus" between state action and the object of the law.
Franco-Dutch War: French troops defeated Austrian and Brandenburg forces at the Battle of Turckheim in Alsace.

image.caption: Date 5 January 1675 Location Turckheim (now in Alsace , France) 48°5′9″N 7°16′12″E ﻿ / ﻿ 48.08583°N 7.27000°E ﻿ / 48.08583; 7.27000 Result French victory

facts.text: Nellie Tayloe Ross was inaugurated as Governor of Wyoming, the first woman to serve as the governor of a U.S. state.

links.title: List of female governors in the United States

facts.text: The bulk carrier Lake Illawarra struck a bridge over the River Derwent in Hobart, Australia, causing the deaths of seven of the ship's crewmen and five motorists on the bridge.
The Troubles: In response to the killings of six Catholics the previous night, South Armagh Republican Action Force gunmen killed ten Protestants in County Armagh, Northern Ireland.
The embassy of the United States to Somalia was evacuated by helicopter airlift days after violence enveloped Mogadishu during the Somali Civil War.

links.title: Embassy of the United States, Mogadishu

facts.text: Stefan Dečanski was crowned King of Serbia, succeeding his half-brother Stefan Konstantin, whom he later defeated in battle.
Four years before the fall of Constantinople, Constantine XI Palaiologos assumed the throne as the last Byzantine emperor.
King Henry VIII of England married his fourth wife, Anne of Cleves; the marriage was annulled six months later.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of Liebster Immanuel, Herzog der Frommen, a chorale cantata for Epiphany.

links.title: Liebster Immanuel, Herzog der Frommen, BWV 123

facts.text: The worst storm to impact Ireland in 300 years damaged or destroyed more than 20 per cent of houses in Dublin with 100-knot (190 km/h) winds.
German geophysicist Alfred Wegener presented his theory of continental drift, the precursor of plate tectonics, to the German Geological Society.
The inaugural Asian Socialist Conference, an organisation of socialist political parties, opened in Rangoon with 177 delegates, observers and fraternal guests.
National Airlines Flight 2511, traveling from New York City to Miami, exploded in mid-air due to a bomb placed by an unknown party, resulting in the deaths of all 34 people on board.
Two-time American Olympic figure-skating medalist Nancy Kerrigan was hit on the leg with a police baton by an assailant hired by the ex-husband of her rival Tonya Harding.
The first episode of the documentary series Benefits Street aired on Channel 4, prompting discussion in the United Kingdom about welfare dependency.

Supporters of then-outgoing U.S. president Donald Trump attack the United States Capitol to disrupt certification of the 2020 presidential election, resulting in five deaths and evacuation of the U.S. Congress.

links.title: Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election
2021 United States Electoral College vote count

facts.text: Harold Godwinson, the last Anglo-Saxon monarch before the Norman Conquest, was crowned King of England.
The oldest European school of higher learning in the Americas, the Colegio de Santa Cruz, was founded in Tlatelolco, Mexico City.

links.title: Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco

facts.text: Italian educator Maria Montessori opened her first school and day-care centre for working-class children in Rome, employing a philosophy of education that now bears her name.
During his State of the Union address, U.S. president Franklin D. Roosevelt presented his Four Freedoms (composite poster depicted) as fundamental freedoms that all people ought to enjoy.
A brawl broke out between players, fans, and police officers during an ice hockey game between the Philadelphia Flyers and the St. Louis Blues in Philadelphia.

Through his telescope, Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei made the first observation of Jupiter's Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, although he was not able to distinguish the first two until the following night.
The Bank of North America opened in Philadelphia as the de facto first central bank of the United States.
The Italian tricolour was first adopted as an official flag by the government of the Cispadane Republic.
The Marconi International Marine Communication Company specified CQD (audio featured) as the distress signal to be used by its operators.
French physicist Marguerite Perey identified francium, the last element to be discovered in nature rather than by synthesis.
Air National Guard pilot Thomas Mantell, flying in pursuit of an alleged UFO, was killed when his P-51 Mustang crashed near Fort Knox, Kentucky.
Marian Anderson became the first African-American to perform with the Metropolitan Opera in New York.
The People's Army of Vietnam captured Phnom Penh, marking the end of large-scale fighting in the Cambodian–Vietnamese War.

Representatives of Iranian leader Ruhollah Khomeini delivered a letter to Mikhail Gorbachev, inviting him to consider Islam as an alternative to communism, and predicting the dissolution of the Soviet Bloc.
The Fourth Republic of Ghana was inaugurated with Jerry Rawlings, the country's former military ruler, as president.
In Nag Hammadi, Egypt, Muslim gunmen opened fire on a crowd of Coptic Christians leaving church after attending Christmas Liturgy, killing eight of them, as well as one Muslim bystander.
A hot air balloon flight from Carterton, New Zealand, collided with a power line while landing, causing it to crash and killing all eleven people on board.
After 253 days without an operational government, a second round of investiture votes produced Spain's first coalition government since the Second Republic.
The Parliament of 1327, which was instrumental in the transfer of the English Crown from King Edward II to his son, Edward III, began at the Palace of Westminster.
Australian aviator Guy Menzies flew from Sydney to New Zealand's West Coast, making the first solo trans-Tasman flight.

image.caption: Born Guy Lambton Menzies ( 1909-08-20 ) 20 August 1909 Drummoyne, New South Wales , Australia

facts.text: An article entitled " Iran and Red and Black Colonization " was published in the newspaper Ettela'at attacking Ruhollah Khomeini, then in exile in Iraq.

links.title: Iran and Red and Black Colonization

facts.text: In one of the most famous upsets in FA Cup history, Sutton United, a team in the fifth tier of English league football, defeated top-tier Coventry City.
Lotario dei Conti was elected as Pope Innocent III; he later worked to restore papal power in Rome.
Scottish student Thomas Aikenhead became the last person in Great Britain to be executed for blasphemy.
American statistician Herman Hollerith received a patent for his electromechanical tabulating machine for punched-card data.
Blackstone Library, the first branch of the Chicago Public Library system, was dedicated.

image.caption: Interactive map of the Blackstone Library area

facts.text: U.S. president Woodrow Wilson announced his Fourteen Points for a moral cause and for post– World War I peace in Europe.
Reza Shah issued the Kashf-e hijab decree, ordering Iranian police to remove hijabs from any women in public.
Five Evangelical Christian missionaries from the United States were killed by the Huaorani in the rainforest of Ecuador shortly after making contact with them.
Following Pakistan's defeat in the Bangladesh Liberation War, President Zulfikar Ali Bhutto released Bangladeshi politician Sheikh Mujibur Rahman from prison in response to international pressure.
Three bombs attributed to Armenian nationalists exploded across Moscow, killing seven people and injuring 37 people.
In Trans-en-Provence, France, a local farmer reported a UFO sighting claimed to be "perhaps the most completely and carefully documented sighting of all time".
Jared Lee Loughner opened fire at a public meeting held by U.S. representative Gabby Giffords in Tucson, Arizona, killing six people and injuring twelve others.
George Frideric Handel 's opera Ariodante premiered at the Covent Garden Theatre in London.
George Washington delivered the first State of the Union address in New York City, then the provisional capital of the United States.
The New Deal for Aborigines was formally announced by the Australian government, providing for full civil rights for Indigenous Australians in exchange for cultural assimilation.
Jeremy Wade Delle committed suicide in his high-school class in Richardson, Texas, an event that inspired the Pearl Jam song " Jeremy ".

Gunmen from an offshoot of the Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda attacked the bus transporting the Togo national football team to the Africa Cup of Nations in Angola, killing three people.

links.title: Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda

facts.text: War of the First Coalition: The siege of Kehl by Habsburg and Württembergian forces ended when French troops withdrew from their fortifications.
An earthquake registering 7.9 M w ruptured part of the San Andreas Fault in central and southern California.
First World War: Troops of the British Empire defeated Ottoman forces at the Battle of Rafa on the Sinai – Palestine border.
The Presidential Council for Minority Rights, an appointed body to review legislation and prevent discrimination against minorities, was created in Singapore.
The Los Angeles Lakers of the National Basketball Association lost to the Milwaukee Bucks, ending a 33-game winning streak, the longest in major American professional team sports.
The Great Storm spawned the first of 45 tornadoes over a three-day period in the Southeastern United States.
Iranian Revolution: Protests took place in Qom after an article insulting Ruhollah Khomeini was published.

links.title: Iran and Red and Black Colonization

facts.text: Representatives from the United States and Iraq met at the Geneva Peace Conference to find a peaceful resolution to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait.
Radio astronomers Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail announced the discovery of two pulsar planets orbiting PSR B1257+12 (depicted), the first confirmed detection of exoplanets.
In poor weather conditions, Iran Air Flight 277 crashed near Urmia Airport, Iran, killing 78 of the 105 people on board.
Contaminated beer served at a funeral in Tete Province, Mozambique, killed 75 people and made at least 230 others ill.
World War I: A meeting of the German Crown Council decided upon the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare.
Seawise University, formerly RMS Queen Elizabeth, an ocean liner that sailed the Atlantic for Cunard Line, caught fire in Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong.
U.S. representative Raymond Lederer was convicted of bribery and conspiracy for his role in the Abscam scandal, but continued to serve his term for three more months.
First Chechen War: Chechen separatists launched raids in the city of Kizlyar, Dagestan, which turned into a massive hostage crisis involving thousands of civilians.
A hostage situation, related to the Charlie Hebdo shooting, occurred at a Jewish market in Vincennes.
Pope Fabian, said to have been chosen by the Holy Spirit when a dove landed on his head, began his papacy.
Moldavian–Ottoman Wars: Stephen the Great led Moldavian forces to defeat an Ottoman attack under Hadım Suleiman Pasha near Vaslui in present-day Romania.
New Orleans, the first steamship on the Mississippi River, arrived at New Orleans to complete its maiden voyage.
Service began on the Metropolitan Railway (construction depicted) between Paddington and Farringdon Street, today the oldest segment of the London Underground.
The first great gusher of the Texas oil boom was discovered in the Spindletop oil field near Beaumont.
Lithuanian residents of the Klaipėda Region began a revolt, ahead of a League of Nations decision on their future which they expected to be against their interest.
The science fiction film Metropolis, directed by Fritz Lang, was released in Germany.
Tintin in the Land of the Soviets, the first volume of The Adventures of Tintin by the Belgian cartoonist Hergé, began serialisation.

links.title: Tintin in the Land of the Soviets

facts.text: The first session of the United Nations General Assembly convened at the Methodist Central Hall in London with representatives from 51 member states.

links.title: Member states of the United Nations

facts.text: The Braer Storm, the strongest extratropical cyclone ever recorded in the North Atlantic, reached peak intensity.
A general strike began in Guinea as an attempt to force President Lansana Conté to resign, eventually resulting in the appointment of two new prime ministers.
After the death of his guardian John I Tzimiskes, Basil II became the effective ruler and senior emperor of the Byzantine Empire.
Philip the Good established the Order of the Golden Fleece, referred to as the most prestigious, exclusive, and expensive order of chivalry in the world.
Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition: Seven survivors of the Ross Sea party were rescued after being stranded for several months.
Greco-Italian War: The Greek army captured the strategically important Klisura Pass in Albania.
The first session of the United Nations General Assembly convened in London with representatives from the original 51 member states.

links.title: First session of the United Nations General Assembly
Member states of the United Nations

facts.text: Sir Clive Sinclair launched the Sinclair C5 personal electric vehicle, "one of the great marketing bombs of postwar British industry", which later became a cult collectable despite its commercial failure.
Arauco War: The Mapuche-Huilliche of southern Chile defeated a slave-hunting Spanish army at the Battle of Río Bueno.
The most powerful earthquake recorded in Italy struck the island of Sicily, causing 60,000 deaths and prompting a period of architectural revival.
German-born British astronomer William Herschel discovered two Uranian moons, later named Oberon and Titania by his son John.
A conflagration in Savannah, Georgia, destroyed more than 400 buildings and caused millions of dollars in damages.
American Civil War: The Battle of Arkansas Post concluded with the Union Army capturing a fort from Confederate forces near the mouth of the Arkansas River.
Immigrant textile workers in Lawrence, Massachusetts, went on strike in response to a pay cut corresponding to a new state law shortening the working week.
The Karluk, the flagship of the Canadian Arctic Expedition, sank after being crushed by ice.
Troops from France and Belgium invaded the Ruhr to force the Weimar Republic to pay reparations in the aftermath of World War I.

Louis B. Mayer, head of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, hosted 36 people involved in the film industry at a banquet, where he announced the creation of what would become the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

links.title: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

facts.text: Italian-American journalist and trade-union activist Carlo Tresca, a leading public opponent of the Mafia infiltration of unions, was assassinated in New York City.

In a landmark report, U.S. surgeon general Luther Terry issued a warning that tobacco smoking may be hazardous to health, concluding that it has a causative role in lung cancer, chronic bronchitis, and other illnesses.

After Chicago police detective Jon Burge was discovered to have extracted forced confessions from more than 200 suspects, the governor of Illinois commuted the death sentences of 167 prisoners and pardoned four others.
French special forces failed in an attempted rescue of a DGSE agent, who had been taken hostage in 2009 by al-Shabaab, in Bulo Marer, Somalia.
Theodora Porphyrogenita became the sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire after the death of her brother-in-law Constantine IX Monomachos.
The People's Republic of Albania was proclaimed, with Enver Hoxha as the country's de facto head of state.
Students at the University of Georgia rioted in an attempt to prevent the attendance of two African-American students.
The Gateway Bridge in Brisbane, Australia, opened as the largest prestressed-concrete, single-box bridge in the world.
Several thousand North Korean migrant workers in Helong engaged in civil unrest, including a factory occupation and the taking of managers as hostages, due to unpaid wages.

links.title: 2024 Helong North Korean migrant workers unrest

facts.text: Bayinnaung, who later assembled what was probably the largest empire in the history of mainland Southeast Asia, was crowned as the king of the Burmese Toungoo dynasty.
The fort at Allahabad was surrendered to the forces of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.
Mission Santa Clara de Asís, a Spanish mission in California that formed the basis of both the city of Santa Clara and Santa Clara University, was established by the Franciscans.
The foundation stone of Saint Fin Barre's Cathedral in Cork was laid.
Anglo-Zulu War: Natal Native Contingent and British troops defeated Zulu forces in the Action at Sihayo's Kraal.
During a storm, the crew of Lynmouth Lifeboat Station transported their 10-ton lifeboat 15 mi (24 km) overland in order to rescue a damaged schooner.
An underground explosion at a coal mine in Staffordshire, England, killed 155 men and boys.
Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah was overthrown by rebels led by John Okello, ending 200 years of Arab dominance in Zanzibar.
Seventy-three-year-old psychology professor James Bedford became the first person to be cryonically preserved with intent of future resuscitation.
Comet McNaught reached perihelion, becoming the brightest comet in over 40 years, with an apparent magnitude of −5.5.
Iranian physicist Massoud Ali-Mohammadi was assassinated while leaving his home for the University of Tehran, where he was a professor.
Basiliscus became Byzantine emperor after Zeno was forced to flee Constantinople.
John Rennie 's scheme to defend St Mary's Church in Reculver from coastal erosion was abandoned in favour of demolition, despite the church being an exemplar of Anglo-Saxon architecture.
The National Trust, a conservation organisation in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, was founded.
Oswald Boelcke and Max Immelmann became the first German aviators to be awarded the Pour le Mérite, Germany's highest military honour.
An earthquake registering 7.0 M w struck Haiti, killing more than 100,000 people.
Pope Eugene IV promulgated the papal bull Sicut dudum, forbidding the enslavement of the native Guanche of the Canary Islands by the Spanish.
French Revolutionary Wars: A naval battle off the coast of Brittany between two British frigates and a French ship of the line ended with hundreds of deaths when the latter ran aground.
First Anglo-Afghan War: William Brydon, an assistant surgeon in the British Army, was the sole European of the 14,000 people retreating from Kabul to Jalalabad who evaded capture or death.
Welsh physician William Price was arrested for attempting to cremate his deceased infant son; this eventually led to the passing of the Cremation Act 1902 by Parliament.
The Treaty of Cahuenga was signed, informally ending the fighting of the Mexican–American War in California.
About 30,000 people were killed when an earthquake struck the Province of L'Aquila in Italy.
Nine Moscow doctors were accused of a plot to poison members of the Soviet political and military leadership.
Togo's first president, Sylvanus Olympio, was assassinated by military officers in a coup d'état led by Emmanuel Bodjollé, Étienne Eyadéma, and Kléber Dadjo.
American singer Johnny Cash recorded his landmark album At Folsom Prison live at Folsom State Prison in California.
British rock band Led Zeppelin released their first album, Led Zeppelin, in the United States.
Ghanaian military officer Ignatius Kutu Acheampong led a coup to overthrow Prime Minister Kofi Abrefa Busia and President Edward Akufo-Addo.
Bernice Gera won a sex-discrimination lawsuit against the National Association of Professional Baseball Leagues, allowing her to become the first female professional baseball umpire.
Steve Ballmer replaced Bill Gates as the chief executive officer of Microsoft.
The Italian cruise ship Costa Concordia ran aground on a reef and capsized off Isola del Giglio, Tuscany.
British troops captured Fort Peter in St. Marys, in the only battle of the War of 1812 to take place in the state of Georgia.
The first Feminist Congress of Yucatán began in Mérida, Mexico, to propose reforms for women's social, educational, and legal rights.

image.caption: Native name Primer Congreso Feminista de Yucatán

facts.text: In the first recorded instance of strike action by Catholic laity against the clergy, gravediggers at Calvary Cemetery in Queens, New York City, went on strike.
The first of two large earthquakes in the span of a month struck El Salvador, killing at least 944 people and destroying over 100,000 homes.
The trans-Neptunian object 208996 Achlys was discovered by Chad Trujillo and Michael E. Brown at Palomar Observatory, California.
King Andrew III died without any male heirs, ending the Árpád dynasty, which had ruled Hungary since the late 9th century.
Philip V, the first Bourbon king of Spain, abdicated in favour of his seventeen-year-old eldest son, who became Louis I.
Sweden and Denmark–Norway signed the Treaty of Kiel, whereby Frederick VI of Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden in return for the Swedish holdings in Pomerania.
Giacomo Puccini 's opera Tosca, based on the play La Tosca by French dramatist Victorien Sardou, premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome.
Norway claimed Queen Maud Land, a 2.7-million km 2 (1.0-million sq mi) region of Antarctica, as a dependent territory.
A major fire and series of explosions aboard the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier USS Enterprise killed 28 sailors, injured 314 others, and destroyed 15 aircraft.
The self-proclaimed Republic of Biafra in southeastern Nigeria surrendered to the federal government less than three years after declaring independence, ending the Nigerian Civil War.
Elvis Presley 's concert Aloha from Hawaii via Satellite was broadcast live to audiences in Asia and Oceania.

In the " Minneapolis Miracle ", American football player Stefon Diggs caught a 61-yard (56 m) touchdown pass that secured the Minnesota Vikings ' victory in the National Football Conference divisional playoff game.
Dutch–Portuguese War: The Dutch siege of Malacca against the Portuguese ended when Dutch troops seized the city's citadel (depicted).
An earthquake registering 6.2 M w struck Kingston, Jamaica, resulting in approximately 1,000 deaths.
Vietnam War: United States and Australian troops ended Operation Crimp; during the military operation, troops discovered an extensive tunnel network used by the Viet Cong.
Austrian logician Kurt Gödel, who suffered from an obsessive fear of being poisoned, died of starvation after his wife was hospitalized and unable to cook for him.
Arab Spring: Tunisian president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali fled the country after several violent protests.
War of 1812: The American frigate USS President, commanded by Commodore Stephen Decatur, was captured by a squadron of four British frigates.
American Civil War: The Union Army captured Fort Fisher, the last seaport of the Confederacy.
In Regent's Park, London, the ice on the lake broke, plunging skaters into the water and causing 40 deaths from drowning or hypothermia.
A large molasses tank in Boston, Massachusetts, burst and a wave of molasses rushed through the streets, killing 21 people and injuring 150 others.
A teenage girl in Banneux, Belgium, reported the first of several Marian apparitions, now known as Our Lady of Banneux.
Spanish Civil War: Nationalist and Republican forces both withdrew after suffering heavy losses at the Second Battle of the Corunna Road.

links.title: Second Battle of the Corunna Road

facts.text: The mutilated corpse of the Black Dahlia, a 22-year-old woman whose murder is one of the most famous unsolved crimes in the United States, was found in Leimert Park, Los Angeles.
The highest-capacity office building in the world, the headquarters of the United States Department of Defense known as the Pentagon, was dedicated.
The Green Bay Packers defeated the Kansas City Chiefs in the American football championship game now known as Super Bowl I.
American serial killer Dennis Rader, also known as the "BTK killer", murdered his first four victims.
Portugal and the nationalist factions UNITA, the MPLA and the FNLA signed the Alvor Agreement, ending the Angolan War of Independence.
The American serial police-procedural television show Hill Street Blues aired its pilot episode, " Hill Street Station ".
In British Hong Kong, hundreds of Europeans were non-lethally poisoned by arsenic in bread from a locally owned bakery, leading to geopolitical tension.
Wilson Bentley took the first known photograph of a snowflake by attaching a bellows camera to a microscope.

image.caption: Born Wilson Alwyn Bentley ( 1865-02-09 ) February 9, 1865 Jericho, Vermont , United States

facts.text: At least 10,700 people died when a magnitude-8.0 earthquake struck Nepal and the Indian state of Bihar.
The Victoria Cross for Australia was instituted, making Australia the first Commonwealth realm with a separate Victoria Cross award in its honours system.
US Airways Flight 1549 struck a flock of Canada geese during its climb out from New York City and made an emergency landing in the Hudson River (featured).
Construction was completed on the Buffalo Bill Dam, then the tallest dam in the world, on the Shoshone River in the U.S. state of Wyoming.
Ilse Koch, wife of Karl-Otto Koch, the Nazi commander of the Buchenwald and Majdanek concentration camps, was sentenced to life imprisonment by a West German court.
The Derveni papyrus, the oldest surviving manuscript in Europe, was discovered in Macedonia in northern Greece.
The Republic of Biafra surrendered following a failed attempt at secession from Nigeria, ending the Nigerian Civil War.
The first edit to the internet encyclopedia Wikipedia was made.
Eleanor of Provence received permission from her son King Edward I of England to expel Jews from the towns of Worcester, Marlborough, Cambridge and Gloucester.

links.title: History of the Jews in England (1066–1290)

facts.text: American Revolutionary War: The Royal Navy gained their first major naval victory over their European enemies in the war when they defeated a Spanish squadron in the Battle of Cape St. Vincent.
Peninsular War: French forces under Jean-de-Dieu Soult attacked the British amphibious evacuation under Sir John Moore at Corunna in Galicia, Spain.
A pumping engine at a colliery in New Hartley, England, broke and fell down the shaft, trapping miners below and resulting in 204 deaths.
Despite being blind in one eye, ice hockey player Frank McGee set the record for most goals in a Stanley Cup game when he scored 14 against the Dawson City Nuggets.
The League of Nations, the first worldwide intergovernmental organization with a focus on peace and security, held its first council meeting in Paris.
TWA Flight 3 crashed into Potosi Mountain in Nevada, killing actress Carole Lombard and all of the other 21 people on board.

World War II: During the Battle of Bataan, U.S. Army sergeant Jose Calugas organized a squad of volunteers to man an artillery position under heavy fire, an action that later earned him the Medal of Honor.

image.caption: Born ( 1907-12-29 ) December 29, 1907 Barrio Tagsing, Leon , Iloilo , Philippine Islands

facts.text: The musical Hello, Dolly! opened at the St. James Theatre on Broadway, and went on to win ten Tony Awards, a record that stood for 37 years.
In Mrauk U, Myanmar, police fired into a crowd protesting the ban of an event to mark the anniversary of the end of the Kingdom of Mrauk U, resulting in seven deaths and twelve injuries.
Sir Francis Bigod began an armed rebellion against King Henry VIII and the English Parliament.
The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, establishing the United States Civil Service, was enacted by the U.S. Congress.
World War II: Adolf Hitler and his staff moved into the Führerbunker in Berlin, where he would eventually commit suicide.
After gunmen took hostages the previous night at a restaurant in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, government commandos stormed the premises to bring the situation to an end.
Turkish Airlines Flight 6491 crashed in Manas International Airport after the flight overflew the entire runway, which resulted in 39 deaths.
Gregory XI, the last Avignon pope, entered Rome after a four-month journey from Avignon, returning the papacy to its original city.
Representatives of Catherine de' Medici, the regent of France, drew up the Edict of Saint-Germain, providing limited tolerance to the Protestant Huguenots.
Lorrin A. Thurston and the Citizens' Committee of Public Safety led the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom and the government of Queen Liliʻuokalani.

image.caption: Date January 17, 1893 ; 133 years ago ( 1893-01-17 ) Location Honolulu , Hawaii Result United States victory Surrender of the Hawaiian Kingdom Queen Liliʻuokalani relinquishes power Provisional Government , later renamed a Republic , established Hawaii organized into a territory , then a state of the United States

facts.text: Robert Falcon Scott 's ill-fated Terra Nova Expedition reached the South Pole, only to find that Roald Amundsen 's team had beaten them by 33 days.
The Volstead Act went into effect, beginning the prohibition of alcohol in the United States.
World War II: Australian troops advanced along the northern part of Bougainville Island (in present-day Papua New Guinea) and began fighting Japanese forces in the Battle of Tsimba Ridge.

Indonesian National Revolution: The Renville Agreement between the Netherlands and Indonesian republicans was ratified, in an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to resolve disputes arising from the Linggadjati Agreement of 1946.
The Drudge Report became the first news source to break the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal to the public.
In Little Saigon, California, a series of protests began when the owner of a video rental store displayed an image of Ho Chi Minh.
Mount Nyiragongo, a volcano in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, began an eruption that killed hundreds and left about 120,000 people homeless in the nearby town of Goma.
On James Cook 's second voyage, his vessel HMS Resolution became the first vessel to cross the Antarctic Circle.
Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg, who had saved thousands of Jews from the Holocaust, was taken into Soviet custody during the Siege of Budapest and was never seen in public again.
Three days before leaving office, U.S. president Dwight D. Eisenhower delivered a farewell speech to the nation, in which he warned about the dangers of the military–industrial complex.
Patrick Purdy opened fire in an elementary school in Stockton, California, killing 5 and wounding 32 others.
The first spate of violence between Muslims and Christians began in Jos, Nigeria, and would end in more than 200 deaths.
The young child Leo II became the sole Byzantine emperor upon the death of his grandfather Leo I.
The armed tender HMS Supply, the first ship of the First Fleet, arrived at Botany Bay, Australia.
The German Empire was formed by the unification of previously independent German states, under the rule of Kaiser Wilhelm I.
Construction of the United Nations Military Cemetery began in Busan, South Korea.
Iranian Shia cleric Navvab Safavi, founder of the fundamentalist group Fada'iyan-e Islam, was executed for attempting to assassinate Prime Minister Hossein Ala'.
Willie O'Ree of the Boston Bruins played his first game in the National Hockey League, becoming the first black Canadian to compete in the NHL.
In response to months of nationwide student protests, thousands of Japanese police stormed the University of Tokyo.

Thirty years after his death, the International Olympic Committee presented commemorative medals to the family of American athlete Jim Thorpe, who had been stripped of his gold medals for playing semi-professional baseball before the 1912 Summer Olympics.
In a sting operation conducted by the FBI, Marion Barry, the mayor of Washington, D.C., was arrested for possession of crack cocaine.
An oil pipeline explosion killed 137 people in Tlahuelilpan, Mexico.
Francisco Pizarro founded Ciudad de los Reyes (present-day Lima, Peru) as the capital of the lands he conquered for the Spanish crown.
Japanese prime minister Ōkuma Shigenobu issued the Twenty-One Demands to China in a bid to increase Japan's power in East Asia.
World War II: In Operation Iskra, the Red Army established a narrow land corridor to Leningrad, partially easing the protracted German siege of the city.
Members of the Lumbee tribe arrived to protest at a Ku Klux Klan rally near Maxton, North Carolina, which turned into an armed confrontation between the two groups.
Singaporean communist activist Tan Chay Wa was executed, leading to a much-publicised trial of his brother for engraving "subversive" material on the gravestone.
Hundred Years' War: The siege of Rouen ended with English troops capturing the city from Norman French forces.
The Batavian Republic was established the day after William V fled the Dutch Republic as a result of the Batavian Revolution in Amsterdam.
A deed was recorded for David Hanbury to sell Island No. 2 in northern California to his brother John for $10 ($358.33 in 2025 ).
The American Civil Liberties Union was founded by the directors of the National Civil Liberties Bureau.
Iva Toguri, convicted of treason for broadcasting Japanese propaganda, was granted a full pardon by U.S. president Gerald Ford.

image.caption: Born Iva Ikuko Toguri ( 1916-07-04 ) July 4, 1916 Los Angeles , California, U.S.

facts.text: A tank barge and a tug grounded on a beach in Rhode Island, causing a spill of an estimated 828,000 U.S. gallons (3.13 million litres) of home heating oil.
In the deadliest aviation accident in Slovak history, an Antonov An-24 operated by the Slovak Air Force crashed in northern Hungary, killing 42 of the 43 people on board.

links.title: 2006 Slovak Air Force Antonov An-24 crash

facts.text: Turkish-Armenian journalist and human-rights activist Hrant Dink was assassinated by a Turkish nationalist in Istanbul.
The Hong Kong–based file-sharing website Megaupload was shut down by the FBI.
War of the League of Cambrai: Troops led by Pope Julius II captured Mirandola (depicted) after a brief siege.

links.title: War of the League of Cambrai

facts.text: World War I: The first major attack of the German bombing campaign against Britain took place when Zeppelins bombed several towns in Norfolk.
The French newspaper L'Aurore revealed that the former Nazi SS officer Klaus Barbie, the "Butcher of Lyon", had been found to be living in Peru.
An earthquake registering 6.8 M s struck northern Himachal Pradesh in India, causing extensive damage to the region.

A four-man team, using only skis and kites, completed a 1,093-mile (1,759 km) trek to reach the Southern Pole of Inaccessibility, the first people to get there since 1967, and the first to do so on foot.
Simon de Montfort summoned local representatives to the Palace of Westminster to attend a parliament, now considered to be the forerunner of the House of Commons of England.

links.title: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester

facts.text: Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná, became the de facto first prime minister of the Empire of Brazil.

links.title: Honório Hermeto Carneiro Leão, Marquis of Paraná

facts.text: The Holocaust: Reinhard Heydrich and other senior Nazi officials met at the Wannsee Conference near Berlin to discuss the implementation of the " Final Solution to the Jewish Question ".
World War II: In an operation that took nearly two months to complete, Germany began the evacuation of at least 1.8 million people from East Prussia in anticipation of the advancing Soviet Red Army.
Bengali student activist Amanullah Asaduzzaman was shot and killed by East Pakistani police, an event that led to the Bangladesh Liberation War.
The Soviet Red Army violently cracked down on Azeri pro-independence demonstrations in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR.
During a national financial crisis, thousands of people protested at the Icelandic parliament in Reykjavík.
A group of Taliban gunmen attacked and took hostages at the Hotel Inter-Continental Kabul, Afghanistan, sparking a 12-hour battle that left at least 21 people dead.
According to legend, Lalli slew Bishop Henry of Finland with an axe on the ice of Lake Köyliönjärvi in Köyliö.
Edward Balliol, whose father John was briefly King of Scotland, gave up his claim to the throne in exchange for an English pension.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of his cantata Meine Seufzer, meine Tränen on the second Sunday after the Epiphany.

The Houston Cougars upset the UCLA Bruins in what became known as the " Game of the Century ", ending the Bruins' 47-game winning streak and establishing college basketball as a sports commodity on American television.

image.caption: UCLA Bruins Houston Cougars Pac-8 Independent (13–0) (14–0) 69 71 Head coach : John Wooden Head coach : Guy Lewis

facts.text: In Washington, D.C., Barack Obama was inaugurated as the first African-American president of the United States.
The Abbasid Caliphate crushed the Alid revolt when a rebel leader was mortally wounded in battle near Basra in present-day Iraq.
French and Indian War: French regulars, Canadien militia and Indigenous forces ambushed Rogers' Rangers forces in the Battle on Snowshoes.
French Revolution: After being found guilty of high treason by the National Convention, Louis XVI was guillotined in Paris.
The First Dáil convened at the Mansion House in Dublin and adopted a declaration of independence calling for the establishment of the Irish Republic.
Mount Lamington, a volcano in Papua New Guinea, erupted and killed more than 2,900 people.
A B-52 bomber carrying four nuclear weapons crashed onto sea ice near Thule Air Base, Greenland, causing localized radioactive contamination.
Tripura, formerly part of the independent Twipra Kingdom, became a state of India.

links.title: States and union territories of India

facts.text: The DeLorean Motor Company completed the first production car of the DMC DeLorean at its factory in Northern Ireland.
The U.S. House of Representatives voted 395–28 to reprimand Newt Gingrich for ethics violations, making him the first Speaker of the House to be so disciplined.

links.title: Speaker of the United States House of Representatives

facts.text: Millions of people participated in the Women's March in Washington, D.C., and around the world to advocate for legislation and policies on human rights and other issues.
A fire at a hotel at the Kartalkaya ski resort in Turkey's Bolu Province results in 78 people killed.
King Edward II of England issued a royal charter confirming Adam de Brome 's foundation of Oriel College, Oxford.
Isaac Isaacs became the first Australian-born governor-general of Australia.
Vietnam War: The People's Army of Vietnam attacked Khe Sanh Combat Base, a U.S. Marines outpost in Quảng Trị province, South Vietnam, starting the Battle of Khe Sanh.
Concorde, an Anglo-French supersonic airliner, began scheduled commercial flights to London, Paris, Bahrain, and Rio de Janeiro.
Demonstrations against alleged corruption in the Albanian government led to the killings of four protesters in Tirana by the Republican Guard.
Eutychius of Constantinople was arrested after he refused Byzantine emperor Justinian I 's order to adopt the tenets of the Aphthartodocetae, a sect of non-Chalcedonian Christians.
Muhammad II became Sultan of Granada after his father 's death in a riding accident.
Anglo-Zulu War: The Zulu forces of King Cetshwayo achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Isandlwana.

image.caption: Date 22 January 1879 Location Isandlwana , Zulu Kingdom 28°21′23″S 30°39′9″E ﻿ / ﻿ 28.35639°S 30.65250°E ﻿ / -28.35639; 30.65250 Result Zulu victory

facts.text: Ramsay MacDonald took office as the first prime minister of the United Kingdom from the Labour Party.

links.title: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

facts.text: World War II: The Battle of Buna–Gona on New Guinea ended with an Allied victory after two months of fighting in which the Japanese fought with a resolve and tenacity not previously encountered.
New York City police arrested George Metesky, better known as the "Mad Bomber", for planting over 30 bombs over 16 years throughout the city.
Apollo 5, the first flight of NASA 's Lunar Module, lifted off from Cape Kennedy Air Force Station.
The U.S. Supreme Court 's landmark decision in Roe v. Wade struck down laws restricting abortion during the first two trimesters of pregnancy.

links.title: Supreme Court of the United States

facts.text: During Super Bowl XVIII, Apple Computer introduced the Macintosh, the first successful personal computer to use a graphical user interface, with the television commercial " 1984 ".
After being convicted of receiving bribes, Pennsylvania state treasurer R. Budd Dwyer shot and killed himself in front of television cameras during a press conference.
Evo Morales was inaugurated as President of Bolivia, becoming the country's first indigenous president.
Croatia held a referendum in which it voted to become a member of the European Union.
The Convention Parliament met to decide the fate of the throne after James II, the last Catholic monarch of England, fled to France following the Glorious Revolution.
The SS Valencia was wrecked off the coast of Vancouver Island, Canada, in a location so treacherous it was known as the Graveyard of the Pacific.
Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev survived what was seen as an assassination attempt, an incident that was not revealed to the public until after the fall of the Soviet Union.
The Boeing 747, the world's first wide-body commercial airliner, entered service for Pan Am on the New York–London route.
After surrounding Mutukula the previous day, Tanzanian forces attacked the town and caused Ugandan forces to flee.

King Louis IX of France issued the Mise of Amiens, a settlement between King Henry III of England and barons led by Simon de Montfort heavily favouring the former, which later led to the Second Barons' War.

links.title: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester

facts.text: James Hamilton killed James Stewart, 1st Earl of Moray, in the first recorded assassination of a head of government using a firearm.
Queen Elizabeth I opened the Royal Exchange in London, giving it its royal title.
Bishop John Carroll purchased a plot of land that would become the home of the future Georgetown University, the oldest Catholic university in the United States.
Elizabeth Blackwell graduated from Geneva Medical College in New York, making her the first woman to receive a medical degree in the United States.
American Indian Wars: In the Marias Massacre, the United States Army killed about 200 Piegan Blackfeet, mostly women, children, and the elderly.
In the most fatal recorded mountaineering accident, 199 of the 210 members of an Imperial Japanese Army unit perished in a blizzard on the Hakkōda Mountains.
Two men committed an armed robbery in Tottenham, London, and led police on a two-hour chase, partially by tram, that ended in the perpetrators' suicides.
Rebels led by John Chilembwe attacked local plantation owners, beginning an uprising regarded as a key moment in the history of Malawi.
World War II: Japan began an invasion of the island of New Britain in the Australian Territory of New Guinea.
American inventor Fred Morrison sold the rights to his "flying disc" to the Wham-O toy company, who later renamed it the " Frisbee "
Madeleine Albright was sworn in as the first female United States Secretary of State, becoming the highest-ranking woman in the history of the U.S. government at that time.

Five people attempted to set themselves on fire in Tiananmen Square, Beijing, an act that many later claimed to have been staged by the Chinese Communist Party to frame Falun Gong and thus escalate their persecution.
American journalist Daniel Pearl was kidnapped and later murdered by al-Qaeda agents in Karachi, Pakistan.
The final signal was detected from the NASA space probe Pioneer 10, then about 12 billion kilometres (7.5 billion miles) from Earth.
The Hongwu Emperor ascended the throne, initiating the Ming dynasty, which would rule China for three centuries.
One of the deadliest earthquakes in history struck Shaanxi, China, resulting in at least 100,000 direct deaths.
The Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia partitioned the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth for the second time.
USS Pueblo was seized by North Korean forces, who claimed that it had violated their territorial waters while spying.
The first version of Mosaic, created by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, was released, becoming the first popular web browser.
The Fatimid Caliphate began their first invasion of Egypt, against the Abbasids, which eventually ended in failure.
The Estates unanimously proclaimed 14-year-old Matthias Corvinus King of Hungary after being persuaded to do so by his uncle Michael Szilágyi.
James W. Marshall discovered gold at Sutter's Mill in Coloma, California, leading to the California gold rush.
The University of Calcutta was established as the first modern university in the Indian subcontinent.
Vietnam War: The 1st Australian Task Force launched Operation Coburg against the North Vietnamese army and the Viet Cong.
Japanese soldier Shoichi Yokoi was found in the jungles of Guam, where he had been hiding since the end of World War II.
Spanish transition to democracy: Neo-fascists attacked an office in Madrid, killing five people and injuring four others.
The Soviet nuclear-powered satellite Kosmos 954 burned up during atmospheric reentry, scattering radioactive debris across Canada's Northwest Territories.
About 20,000 protestors marched in a civil rights demonstration in Forsyth County, Georgia, United States.
Kʼakʼ Tiliw Chan Yopaat dedicated a 65-ton stele, the largest stone known to be quarried by the Maya civilization, at his city of Quiriguá.
Greek military aviators Michael Moutoussis and Aristeidis Moraitinis performed the first naval air mission in history, with a Farman MF.7 hydroplane.
A Boeing B-52 Stratofortress carrying two Mark 39 nuclear weapons broke up in mid-air near Goldsboro, North Carolina; one bomb was recovered intact, the other disintegrated.
Japan launched the Hiten spacecraft, the first lunar probe launched by a country other than the Soviet Union or the United States.
Francis I, a great-great-grandson of Charles V, was crowned king of France in the Reims Cathedral.
English colonists from the Province of Carolina and their native allies began a series of raids against the largely peaceful population of Apalachee in Spanish Florida.
Privateer Amaro Pargo was declared a hidalgo, a member of the Spanish nobility.
Port Egmont, the first British colony in the Falkland Islands, was founded.
Thomas Hardy founded the London Corresponding Society to seek a " radical reform of parliament ", later influencing the reform movements of early-19th-century England.
American journalist Nellie Bly completed a circumnavigation of the globe by land and sea in a then-record-breaking 72 days.

image.caption: Born Elizabeth Jane Cochran ( 1864-05-05 ) May 5, 1864 Burrell Township, Pennsylvania , U.S.

facts.text: Serving as a British armed merchant cruiser, Laurentic was sunk by German naval mines off the northern coast of Ireland, resulting in 354 deaths.
Representatives of the Chetnik movement began a four-day congress to organise political opposition to the Allied support of the communist-led Yugoslav Partisans in Yugoslavia.
South Vietnamese junta leader Nguyễn Cao Kỳ fired his rival Nguyễn Hữu Có while the latter was overseas on a diplomatic visit.
Avianca Flight 52 ran out of fuel on approach to John F. Kennedy International Airport and crashed into the village of Cove Neck, New York, resulting in the deaths of 73 people.
Pakistani national Mir Aimal Kansi shot five people outside the Central Intelligence Agency headquarters in Langley, Virginia, killing two.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam detonated a truck bomb at the sacred Buddhist Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, killing 17 people.
Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity landed on Mars and rolled into Eagle crater, a small crater on the Meridiani Planum.
Ethiopian Airlines Flight 409, en route to Addis Ababa, crashed into the Mediterranean Sea shortly after takeoff from Beirut, Lebanon, killing all 90 people on board.
Avatar, a science-fiction film directed by James Cameron, became the highest-grossing film of all time.
Anne Boleyn (depicted), already pregnant with the future Elizabeth I, secretly married Henry VIII of England in the second of his six marriages.
Idi Amin seized power from Ugandan president Milton Obote in a coup d'état, beginning eight years of military rule.
A team of Norwegian and American scientists launched a Black Brant XII sounding rocket, which was mistaken by Russian forces for a Trident missile.
Three independent observing campaigns announced the discovery of OGLE-2005-BLG-390Lb, a super-Earth 21,500 ± 3,300 light-years away from Earth near the center of the Milky Way.
Arab Spring: The Egyptian revolution began with protests on the "Day of Anger", eventually leading to the removal of President Hosni Mubarak after nearly 30 years of rule.

links.title: Timeline of the Egyptian revolution of 2011

facts.text: Ali, the fourth Rashidun caliph, was assassinated (depicted) by Ibn Muljim, leading to the end of the caliphate.
Livonian War: A Lithuanian surprise attack resulted in a decisive defeat of numerically superior Russian forces.
An earthquake with a moment magnitude of around 9.0 occurred off the Pacific Northwest coast of North America, as evidenced by Japanese records of tsunamis.
Captain Arthur Phillip and the British First Fleet landed at Sydney Cove on the shore of Port Jackson, establishing the first permanent European settlement in Australia.
William Bligh, the governor of New South Wales, was deposed in the only military coup in Australian history.
Mahdist War: The siege of Khartoum ended as Mahdist forces defeated the Egyptian garrison and captured the city.
The 3,106- carat (621 g) Cullinan Diamond, the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found, was discovered at the Premier Mine in Gauteng, South Africa.
A group of Red Guards hung a red lantern atop the tower of the Helsinki Workers' House, symbolically marking the start of the Finnish Civil War.
Hurtig & Seamon's New Burlesque Theater in New York City reopened as the Apollo Theater, becoming one of the nation's premier venues for African-American performers.
Audie Murphy engaged in action at the Colmar Pocket that won him a Medal of Honor and made him one of the most famous and decorated U.S. soldiers of World War II.
The Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the largest aperture optical telescope in the world for 28 years, saw first light.
Indian independence movement: India became a republic under a new constitution, with Rajendra Prasad as president and Jawaharlal Nehru as prime minister.
Spontaneous anti-British riots erupted in Cairo following the killings of 50 Egyptian auxiliary police officers the previous day.
The three Beaumont children disappeared from a beach in Glenelg, South Australia, resulting in one of the country's largest-ever police investigations.
Turkish Airlines Flight 301 crashed while taking off from İzmir Adnan Menderes Airport, killing 67 people.
In a nationally televised press conference, U.S. president Bill Clinton denied having "sexual relations" with intern Monica Lewinsky.
Rioting broke out in Antananarivo, Madagascar, sparking a political crisis that led to the deposal of President Marc Ravalomanana.
A jet fighter crashed at Los Llanos Air Base in Albacete, Spain, killing 11 people and injuring 21 others.
A Sikorsky S-76 helicopter crashed in Calabasas, California, killing all nine people on board, including former basketball player Kobe Bryant and his daughter Gianna.
Commodore Gordon Bremer took formal possession of Hong Kong Island for the United Kingdom at Possession Point.
Oliver Hutchinson appeared on television in inventor John Logie Baird 's first successful demonstration of using the technology to show humans.

JAT Flight 367 exploded in mid-air over Czechoslovakia; the only survivor of the 28 on board, flight attendant Vesna Vulović, fell 10,160 m (33,330 ft), setting the record for surviving the highest fall without a parachute.
Somali Rebellion: Factions led by the warlord Mohamed Farrah Aidid and his rebel group, the United Somali Congress, ousted President Siad Barre.
An earthquake in the Indian state of Gujarat killed at least 20,000 people, injured 167,000 others and destroyed nearly 400,000 homes.
The brothers Stephen and Constantine Lekapenos, having deposed their father as Byzantine emperor a few weeks earlier, were themselves overthrown by Constantine VII, their co-emperor.

French Revolutionary Wars: In the Macau Incident, French and Spanish warships encountered a British Royal Navy escort squadron in the Wanshan Archipelago; subsequent events, including which side retreated, were disputed by the commanders present.
On the advice of John C. Calhoun, President James Monroe asked Congress to organize Indian Territory west of the Mississippi River, laying the groundwork for Indian removal in the United States.
Former members of the overthrown Tokugawa shogunate proclaimed Japan's second-largest island, Hokkaido, to be the independent Republic of Ezo.
A contaminated diphtheria vaccine was used in an Australian immunisation program, leading to the deaths of twelve children and the suspension of immunisation programs in several countries.
The Soviet Red Army liberated about 7,000 prisoners left behind by the Nazis in Auschwitz concentration camp.
South Vietnamese prime minister Trần Văn Hương was removed by the military junta of Nguyễn Khánh.
A fire during a launch simulation for the Apollo 1 mission at Cape Kennedy killed astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee.
Six American diplomats who had evaded capture in the Iran hostage crisis escaped with the help of Canadian government officials to Zürich, Switzerland.
The first selections for the United States National Recording Registry were announced by the Library of Congress.
Porfirio Lobo Sosa became the new president of Honduras, ending a constitutional crisis that had begun in 2009 when Manuel Zelaya was forcibly removed from office.
Arab Spring: The Yemeni Revolution began as more than 16,000 protesters demonstrated in Sanaa to demand governmental changes.
Clement VI issued the papal bull Unigenitus, justifying the power of the pope and the use of indulgences.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of Alles nur nach Gottes Willen, BWV 72, concluding his third Christmas season in Leipzig on the Third Sunday after Epiphany.

links.title: Alles nur nach Gottes Willen, BWV 72
List of church cantatas by liturgical occasion

facts.text: The University of Georgia, the oldest state-chartered public university in the United States, was founded.

links.title: Oldest public university in the United States

facts.text: Mahamane Ousmane, the first democratically elected president of Niger, was deposed by Colonel Ibrahim Baré Maïnassara in a military coup d'état.

links.title: List of heads of state of Niger

facts.text: Astronomers documented H1504+65, a white dwarf in Ursa Minor with the hottest surface temperature known at the time, at 200,000 kelvins (360,000 °F).
Robert de Comines, Earl of Northumbria, was killed in Durham, causing William the Conqueror to embark on a campaign to subjugate northern England.
King Charles VI of France was nearly killed when several other dancers' costumes caught fire during a masquerade ball in Paris.
Nine-year-old Edward VI, the first English monarch to be raised as a Protestant, became king.
Delegates of the Three Nations of Transylvania adopted the Edict of Torda, allowing local communities to elect their preachers freely, in an unprecedented act of religious tolerance.
Anglo-Spanish War: In pursuit of retreating Spanish troops, English soldiers sacked the city of Panama.
The word serendipity, derived from the Persian fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip, was coined by Horace Walpole in a letter to a friend.
The province of Manitoba passed a law that first granted some Canadian women the right to vote.
The largest recorded snowstorm in the history of Washington, D.C., collapsed the Knickerbocker Theatre, killing 98 people.
Choudhry Rahmat Ali published a pamphlet in which he called for the creation of a Muslim state in north-western India that he termed "Pakstan".
World War II: About three hours after Thai bombers raided Sisophon, a ceasefire paused hostilities in the Franco-Thai War.
Three U.S. Air Force pilots aboard an unarmed T-39 Sabreliner were killed when the aircraft was shot down over Erfurt, East Germany, by a Soviet MiG-19.
Tropical Storm Domoina made landfall in southern Mozambique, causing some of the most severe flooding recorded in the region.
Charles V and the estates of the Holy Roman Empire met at the Diet of Worms to discuss Martin Luther and the effects of the Protestant Reformation.
The Lego Group, a Danish toy company, filed a patent in Denmark for the design of Lego bricks.
In Gitarama, Rwanda, local and other government officials initiated a coup to overthrow the monarchy and establish a republic.
U.S. president Ronald Reagan lifted price controls from petroleum products, contributing to the 1980s oil glut.
The Space Shuttle Challenger disintegrated 73 seconds into its tenth mission (video featured), killing all seven crew members.
An Lushan, leader of a revolt against the Tang dynasty and emperor of Yan, was assassinated in a plot involving his own son, An Qingxu.
Sergius III returned from exile to take over the papacy from the deposed antipope Christopher.
The Abbasid caliph, al-Mustakfi, was deposed, and went on to spend the rest of his life as a prisoner in the caliphal palace.
War of the Sixth Coalition: At the Battle of Brienne, both sides' commanders, Napoleon and Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, were nearly captured.
Charles Curtis of Kansas, a citizen of the Kaw Nation, became the first Native American U.S. Senator.
World War II: The Battle of Rennell Island, the last major naval engagement between the United States Navy and the Imperial Japanese Navy during the Guadalcanal campaign, began.
World War II: At least 38 civilians were killed and about a dozen others injured when the Polish village of Koniuchy was attacked by a Soviet partisan unit with a contingent of Jewish partisans.
The Mantra-Rock Dance, called the "ultimate high" of the hippie era, took place in San Francisco, featuring Swami Bhaktivedanta, Janis Joplin, the Grateful Dead, and Allen Ginsberg.
India 's Irfan Pathan became the first bowler to take a Test cricket hat-trick in the opening over of a match.
The Supreme Constitutional Court of Egypt ruled that people who did not adhere to one of the three government-recognised religions were also eligible to receive government identity documents.
Twenty-one people died when SCAT Airlines Flight 760 crashed near Almaty, Kazakhstan.
A lone gunman carried out a mass shooting at a mosque in Quebec City, Canada, killing six people and injuring up to nineteen others.
American poet Edgar Allan Poe 's " The Raven " appeared in The Evening Mirror as the newspaper's first publication attributed to Poe.
Queen Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross, originally to recognise acts of valour by British military personnel during the Crimean War.
Liliʻuokalani, the last monarch and only queen regnant of the Hawaiian Kingdom, ascended the throne.
Mexican Revolution: The Magonista rebellion began when Mexican Liberal Party troops captured the town of Mexicali.
The first major ground engagement of the Gulf War began with the Iraqi invasion of Khafji, Saudi Arabia, recaptured three days later by Coalition forces.
Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Bolesław I, the Piast ruler of Poland, signed the Peace of Bautzen to end the German–Polish War.
Wareru created the Hanthawaddy Kingdom in today's Lower Burma and declared himself king following the collapse of the Pagan Empire.
Low-lying areas flooded around the coasts of the Bristol Channel in southwest England and south Wales, resulting in around 2,000 deaths.
King Charles I, who was defeated in both the First and the Second English Civil Wars, was beheaded for high treason in front of the Banqueting House in London.
Richard Lawrence became the first person to attempt to assassinate a sitting US president when he failed to kill Andrew Jackson at the US Capitol and was subdued by the crowd.
The United States Navy launched USS Monitor, the first American ironclad warship.
In a speech to the Reichstag, Adolf Hitler threatened the " annihilation of the Jewish race in Europe ".
World War II: Allied forces liberated more than 500 prisoners of war from a Japanese POW camp near Cabanatuan in the Philippines.

facts.text: Danish ocean liner MS Hans Hedtoft sank, resulting in the deaths of all 95 passengers and crew.
In a bloodless coup, Nguyễn Khánh overthrew Dương Văn Minh 's military junta in South Vietnam, less than three months after Minh's own coup.
The Troubles: On Bloody Sunday, members of the British Parachute Regiment shot 26 civil-rights protesters in Derry, Northern Ireland, killing at least 13 people.
Kenya Airways Flight 431 crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near Ivory Coast shortly after takeoff, killing 169 on board.
Forty-six years to the day after the sinking of the Danish ocean liner MS Hans Hedtoft, Queen Margrethe II unveiled a memorial in Copenhagen to the 95 passengers and crew who perished.
The World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 pandemic to be a public health emergency of international concern.

links.title: Public health emergency of international concern

facts.text: Two years after his death, Oliver Cromwell 's remains were exhumed for a posthumous execution and his head was placed on a spike above Westminster Hall in London, where it remained until 1685.
Mahatma Gandhi, the political and spiritual leader of India and the Indian independence movement, was fatally shot by Nathuram Godse at Birla House in Delhi.

image.caption: Born Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi ( 1869-10-02 ) 2 October 1869 Porbandar , Kathiawar Agency, British Raj

facts.text: Vietnam War: Forces of the Viet Cong and the Vietnamese People's Army launched the Tet Offensive to strike military and civilian command and control centers throughout South Vietnam.
Varig Flight 967 disappeared shortly after takeoff from Tokyo's Narita International Airport en route to Rio de Janeiro.
The Korea Aerospace Research Institute launched Naro-1, South Korea's first carrier rocket and their first launch vehicle to achieve Earth orbit.
Sylvester I (bust depicted), during whose pontificate many churches in Rome were constructed by Constantine the Great, began his reign as pope.
Sverker II was defeated at the Battle of Lena by Erik Knutsson, who succeeded him as King of Sweden.
Mexican soldiers and Texan militiamen marched into Nacogdoches, Texas, to end the Fredonian Rebellion.

Ute Wars: On behalf of Utah territorial governor Brigham Young, militia leader Daniel H. Wells drafted an order for the Utah Territorial Militia to exterminate Timpanogos men deemed hostile, leading to the Provo River Massacre.
Datu Muhammad Salleh, leader of a series of major disturbances in North Borneo, was shot dead in Tambunan, but his followers did not give up for five more years.
Intense rioting over labour conditions broke out in Glasgow, Scotlan.
A DC-7B operated by Douglas Aircraft collided in mid-air with a U.S. Air Force F-89 and crashed into a schoolyard in Pacoima, California.
Final Fantasy VII, the first video game in the Final Fantasy franchise to use 3-D computer graphics, was released.
Alaska Airlines Flight 261, experiencing problems with its horizontal stabilizer system, crashed in the Pacific Ocean off Anacapa Island, California, killing all 88 people on board.
Emergency officials in Boston mistakenly identified LED placards depicting characters from Aqua Teen Hunger Force as IEDs, causing a panic.
Eighty Years' War: Spanish forces won a crushing victory at the Battle of Gembloux, threatening the States General of the Netherlands and contributing to its move from Brussels to Antwerp.
The London Lock Hospital, the first voluntary hospital specialising in the treatment of venereal diseases, opened.
Aboard NASA 's Mercury-Redstone 2, the chimpanzee Ham became the first hominid to be launched into outer space.
Doug Williams became the first African-American quarterback to play in the Super Bowl, leading the Washington Redskins to victory in Super Bowl XXII.
A gas leak underneath the Pemex Executive Tower in Mexico City caused an explosion that killed at least 37 people and injured another 121.
